title: Augustine of Hippo
summary: Aurelius Augustine (354–430) was a philosopher and theologian from North Africa, bishop of the city of Hippo. In the Confessions he told the story of his life, his attachments and his inner struggles with a frankness unheard of in antiquity, and in The City of God he interpreted history as a contest between two kinds of love. His thoughts on time, memory, will and love influenced all of Western philosophy — from Descartes to Heidegger and Arendt.
onEmotions: Augustine argued with the Stoics, who considered strong feelings diseases of the soul. For him all feelings are forms of love: love reaching for what it loves is desire; love possessing it is joy; love fleeing what is contrary to it is fear; love feeling what is contrary to it is sorrow. So what matters is not to suppress a feeling but to understand what we love and how; rightly ordered love — the "order of love" (ordo amoris) — he considered the essence of virtue. Augustine saw the highest aim of love in God, but his observations on the restless heart, memory, habit and time hold true for the non-believing reader as well.

anxiety.text: "Our heart is restless until it rests in You" — this line stands on the very first page of Augustine's Confessions. He knew better than most a restlessness that won't let you settle, and he saw nothing shameful in it. For Augustine this is not a malfunction but a sign that a human being carries a longing greater than any single thing can satisfy; he himself saw the ultimate aim of that longing in God. But his thought can be useful to a reader outside faith too: anxiety often says not that something is wrong with you, but that you want something very much — security, meaning, something to lean on. Augustine didn't muffle his restless heart; all his life he questioned it: what exactly is it looking for? A desire that has been named is less frightening than a nameless anxiety.
anxiety.practice: Put your palm on your chest, feel your heart beating, and ask it, as Augustine did: "What are you looking for?" Give three different answers under your breath and simply listen to them.

quote.text: You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.
quote.author: Aurelius Augustine

fear.text: "Love fleeing what is contrary to it is fear," Augustine wrote in The City of God. When something dear is under threat, fear comes naturally: all feelings, for Augustine, are forms of love. And in one of his early works he notes that fear essentially has a single cause: dread of losing what we love or of not obtaining what we hope for. Your fear is the other side of attachment. It shows what matters to you. Augustine didn't demand that we stop being afraid; he asked what exactly we love and what we lean on. When you see love behind fear, it becomes easier to talk with it.
fear.practice: Say under your breath: "I'm afraid because I love…" — and finish the sentence. See which love stands behind your fear.

sadness.text: "Jesus wept" — Augustine recalled this short Gospel verse when arguing with the Stoics, for whom strong feelings were diseases of the soul. Your sadness, in his view, is legitimate and does not demean you. Augustine objected: in The City of God he writes that sorrow is love feeling what it does not want, and that everything depends not on the feeling itself but on what a person loves. Complete unfeelingness he considered not a virtue but rather a hardening of the soul into stone. So your sadness is not a mistake to be corrected quickly. It says that somewhere nearby there is a love that is hurting right now.
sadness.practice: Ask yourself: what, or whom, or which part of my life is this sadness about? Write down one word without explaining it: for Augustine, behind it stands a love that is hurting right now.

grief.text: "I had become a great question to myself," Augustine writes of the days after his young friend's death, and only tears were sweet to him then. Grief is one of the deepest wounds, and he knew it from within. Everything around him became torment: his hometown, his father's house — everything reminded him of the one who was gone, and nothing could tell him any more, as when his friend had merely been away, "He'll be here soon." He isn't ashamed of this and doesn't hurry himself. Later, after his mother's death, he held back his tears for a long time — and when he finally allowed himself to weep, his heart found rest in them. His experience says: grief need not be hidden or hurried through. Tears are the language of love.
grief.practice: Allow yourself a few minutes today when you don't have to hold yourself together. If tears come, let them, as they came to Augustine after his mother's death; if not, simply recall one living detail about the person who is gone.

loneliness.text: "Out of such small things souls are fused into one," Augustine wrote of the friends he read, laughed and argued with, without hostility. Loneliness can be sharp, even among people, and it doesn't make you any less. Augustine valued friendship enormously and described it tenderly. In Book IV of the Confessions he recalls what comforted him after his loss: talking and laughing with friends, reading together, being able to fool around together and be serious together, sometimes disagreeing without hostility, teaching one another and learning, missing those who were away and joyfully welcoming those who arrived. Augustine has another thought too: he was convinced that God is closer to a person than they are to themselves — so loneliness is never complete. Even outside faith you can take something simple from this: closeness is built from small shared things, not only from big confessions.
loneliness.practice: Pick one small shared thing from Augustine's list — reading together, laughing, a walk — and suggest it to someone this week. That is what souls are fused from.

anger.text: In the Rule he wrote for his community, Augustine warned: don't let anger grow into hatred and make a beam out of a speck. Anger is a strong feeling, and it often rises where something important has been touched. Augustine did not consider anger evil in itself: in The City of God he allows for anger that rises against injustice and wants to set it right. But he saw one danger in it. A speck that is carried inside, nursed and not let go, becomes a beam over time. That's why Augustine advised ending quarrels as quickly as possible. This is not a demand to forgive immediately. It's more an invitation to notice: while anger is fresh, it is still a message about what matters to you, not a verdict on another person.
anger.practice: Ask your anger aloud: "What are you protecting?" — and answer in one word: a boundary, a value, a person. While anger is fresh, it is still a speck, not a beam.

shame.text: As a teenager Augustine and his friends stripped someone's pear tree at night — they didn't need the pears and soon threw them to the pigs — and years later he told the story in detail in the Confessions. Shame makes you want to vanish from sight; he chose the opposite. The question tormented him for a long time: why? And he comes to an honest conclusion: alone he wouldn't have done it — he wanted to belong to the group. What matters is how he speaks of what is shameful: without self-abasement, wanting to understand. The Latin word confessio means for Augustine not only admission but also praise — gratitude that a person has seen the truth about themselves and has not been crushed by it. Shame spoken out, even on paper, loses some of its power.
shame.practice: Write one sentence about what you're ashamed of — the way an understanding chronicler would, without judgment. Then you can erase it: for Augustine, shame spoken even on paper loses some of its power.

guilt.text: Augustine slipped away from his mother by deception, at night, sailing from Carthage to Rome and leaving her in tears on the shore — and he didn't hide it in the Confessions. Guilt says that you care how your actions affect others. Augustine took guilt seriously, but his Confessions show a particular way of living with it. He doesn't hide his mistakes. But he doesn't get stuck in self-flagellation either: he remembers in order to understand how it all happened and to see that life went on and what grew from it. Guilt, for Augustine, is needed not to chew over the past endlessly but to turn toward something better. Guilt, in this perspective, is not a lifelong brand but the beginning of change.
guilt.practice: Imagine this guilt has already been forgiven. What would you do differently tomorrow? Name one small action aloud — Augustine remembered the past in order to turn toward something better.

envy.text: "I have seen and known such an infant: he could not yet speak, but he turned pale and looked bitterly at his foster brother," Augustine writes in the Confessions. Envy, he thought, is one of the earliest human feelings, and everyone knows it. Augustine looks at this without sentimentality, but without malice either: envy appears before we have a chance to choose it. In The City of God he writes that possession of a good is not diminished when someone else shares it with you. There are goods that can be shared without loss — knowledge, joy, friendship, truth. Envy is sharpest where it seems there won't be enough for everyone. Your envy points to what you want — and it's worth checking whether that good would really diminish if someone else had it too.
envy.practice: Name what you envy and ask the Augustinian question: what part of it wouldn't diminish if I had it too? Say that part aloud.

emptiness.text: "I became to myself a land of want," Augustine writes, recalling his youth — a hungry, barren country. When there seems to be nothing inside and nothing fills you, it is hard, and he knew it from within. His thought about emptiness is paradoxical and comforting. For Augustine, evil and emptiness are not an independent force but a lack of good, as shadow is a lack of light. Emptiness doesn't prove there is nothing in you — it shows the place where something is missing. And the fact that you feel this lack already means a longing for fullness is alive in you. Augustine considered this longing the deepest thing in a person and called its goal God. But even without that, you can start with a simple question: what exactly is missing right now?
emptiness.practice: Picture your emptiness as a cup and ask: what is it waiting to be filled with? Say aloud the first thing that comes — even if it seems small. For Augustine, emptiness is a place where something is missing, not a verdict.

confusion.text: "What then is time? If no one asks me, I know; if I wish to explain it to someone who asks, I do not know," Augustine admits in Book XI of the Confessions. When thoughts won't come together and it's unclear where you are, it is unpleasant, but there is honesty in it. Augustine searched for answers for more than ten years: he was a follower of the Manichaeans, then almost a skeptic who doubted whether anything could be known for certain, then a reader of the Neoplatonists. And he admitted confusion even before the simplest things. For Augustine this is no reason to fall silent but the beginning of inquiry. Confusion, for Augustine, is a sign that you have honestly come up against something bigger than ready-made answers. That's where real searching begins.
confusion.practice: Write down the question that confuses you most right now — as a question, without trying to answer it, the way Augustine wrote down his question about time. A precisely named question already works as a landmark.

quote.text: What then is time? If no one asks me, I know; if I wish to explain it to one who asks, I do not know.
quote.author: Aurelius Augustine

fatigue.text: In Milan, where Augustine was a successful teacher of rhetoric, he was due to deliver a speech in praise of the emperor — full, as he admits, of lies. Walking down the street, worn down by worries, he saw a beggar joking and cheerful — and envied his lightness. Your tiredness is a sign that you've been giving your strength for a long time, and it deserves respect. Augustine realized that he was sinking under the load of ambition that he himself was dragging along and that only kept growing. His conclusion is not that one must drop everything. It is that part of our tiredness comes not from the work itself but from what we work for and how. It's worth asking: what in this load is mine, and what is excess baggage?
fatigue.practice: Walk down the street for a few minutes, like Augustine in Milan, and sort your load as you go: what in it is the work itself, and what is the need to "keep up appearances"? Try setting down one thing from the second part today.

boredom.text: Augustine noticed that when we show a guest the beautiful places of our hometown, we begin to admire them anew ourselves, seeing through the eyes of someone seeing them for the first time. When you have to do the same thing again and again, boredom comes almost inevitably. He wrote a short treatise about this, On the Catechising of the Uninstructed, for a deacon who found it dreary to explain the basics to newcomers again and again. Augustine admits: yes, repeating what you've long known can be boring, and the boredom is passed on to the listener. His advice is unusual. The main remedy for boredom, for Augustine, is not novelty but love and empathy, which make the familiar alive again. Boredom is not a verdict on the task but an invitation to change your angle of view.
boredom.practice: Take one boring task and imagine showing it to a guest who is seeing it for the first time — as Augustine would show someone around his hometown. What would the guest notice?

joy.text: "When many rejoice together, each one's joy is richer: they warm and kindle one another," Augustine writes in the Confessions. Your joy is a gift, and he valued it highly. In Book X of the Confessions he writes that all people without exception want a happy life, and defines it as joy in the truth. He explains: many are willing to deceive, but no one wants to be deceived — so real joy for us is joy in what is genuine, not in appearances. You don't need to do anything with your joy or test how solid it is. You can simply notice what in it is real and what it's about — and let it be.
joy.practice: Tell someone about one thing that made you glad today. Notice how, in Augustine's words, joy grows warmer when it is shared.

love.text: "My weight is my love: wherever I am carried, it is love that carries me," Augustine writes in the Confessions — as heaviness draws a stone down and fire rises up. What you feel stands at the very center of his thought. For him the question was never whether to love — everyone loves. The question is what and how. In The City of God he gives a brief definition of virtue: it is the "order of love" (in Latin ordo amoris) — when each good is loved according to its worth, no more and no less. Augustine saw the summit of this order in the love of God, but a non-believing reader can take much from it too. Your love is a force that steers your life. There's no need to be ashamed of it; it's only worth watching where it is taking you.
love.practice: Stand up and feel your weight — your feet pressing into the floor. Ask yourself the Augustinian question: where is my love carrying me right now? Answer in one word.

gratitude.text: "What do you have that you did not receive?" Augustine returned again and again to this question of the apostle Paul. The gratitude you feel is a quiet and powerful feeling. Augustine's whole Confessions is essentially a book of gratitude: the Latin confessio means for him not only admission but also praise. He gives thanks even for what he can't remember — for his nurse's milk, for the people who cared for him when he was utterly helpless. For him gratitude is not politeness but a way of seeing your life rightly: as woven from gifts, from other people's care and work. Gratitude doesn't make you smaller. It shows that you were never entirely alone in your own story.
gratitude.practice: Name aloud three things or three people without whom you wouldn't be yourself today — starting with the earliest, as Augustine gave thanks even for his nurse's milk.

hope.text: "In this life we are happy in hope rather than in possession," Augustine soberly admits in The City of God. When the present is hard, hope is what holds you. For Augustine hope was one of the three chief virtues, along with faith and love. But his thinking about time makes hope understandable to a non-believer too. The future, Augustine writes, does not yet exist; it exists only in our soul — as expectation. So hope is not a forecast but the way your soul is already turned toward what lies ahead. This is not a reproach to the world: hoping is a normal form of human life, not naivety. Hope already changes how you live now — even if the outcome is still unknown.
hope.practice: Note one thing you hope for, and one small action that already turns toward it today: for Augustine, the future lives in the soul as expectation.

nostalgia.text: Augustine called memory "vast fields and palaces" where the images of everything we have lived through are stored — and he wandered through them, amazed at their depth. He explored the bittersweet feeling you have now with real interest. He was amazed that you can recall a past joy without rejoicing, and a past sorrow without being sad. He even compares memory to "the stomach of the soul": what we lived through is kept there, but without its former taste. Nostalgia is a meeting with something that still lives in you but belongs to another time. For Augustine the past exists only in memory — in the present. So when you remember, you don't go back; you bring the past into today, and it becomes part of who you are now.
nostalgia.practice: Close your eyes and walk through the "palaces of memory," as Augustine did, to one warm room. Linger on a single detail — a sound, a smell, a light — and ask: what from it do I want to bring into today?

craving.text: In Book X of the Confessions Augustine admits that every day he wrangles even with food: it's hard to tell where the necessary ends and appetite begins, because pleasure knows how to pass itself off as need. He knew well the strong wave of desire you feel now, and saw nothing shameful in it. That honesty is valuable: a craving doesn't always show itself as a craving; it disguises itself as "I just need this." Augustine also held that every desire strives toward some good — it points to what we lack. So instead of fighting the wave head-on, you can question it: what are you really looking for — relief, warmth, calm, a breather? The wave rises, peaks and subsides.
craving.practice: When the craving rolls in, rate its strength from 1 to 10 and ask, as Augustine did: "Are you a need — or a pleasure dressed up as need?" After ten minutes, rate it again.

addiction.text: "A chain" — this is what Augustine called habit: from a distorted will comes lust, serving lust becomes habit, and habit that isn't resisted turns into necessity. He described these workings with rare precision, and in his account addiction is not a moral failure but a bondage people find their way out of. The links of this chain, he writes, held him in harsh bondage. There were two wills in him — the old and the new — and they tore his soul apart: he wanted freedom and couldn't take hold of it. Importantly, Augustine did not see the way out in a single effort of will. The turn came to him through other people — through their stories, their example, their support. The way out of the chain is not solitary heroism but something done together.
addiction.practice: Think of who in your life knows what it's like to try to break a chain. If you'd like, talk with such a person, or look in on a mutual-help group: other people's stories helped Augustine.

hangover.text: Augustine tells of his lapses in order to understand, not to execute himself. The morning after is a hard time: the body aches and yesterday keeps spinning in your head. Augustine wrote a lot about how a pleasure that promised joy leaves bitterness and restlessness behind — and about how easy it is to mistake a brief relief for a good. But the main thing in him is how to treat yourself on such mornings. The Confessions are an example of how to look at your own lapses honestly and yet without contempt for yourself. He is sure that a person is not reducible to the worst thing that happened with them. The morning after is not a reason for a verdict but a moment of clarity: what did I actually need yesterday? The answer to that question matters more than shame.
hangover.practice: Pour yourself some water, sit down and write, without judging, as in the Confessions: what did I actually need yesterday? One word is enough.

euphoria.text: At Ostia Augustine and his mother stood at a window overlooking a garden and talked quietly — and at a certain moment it seemed to them that they were touching something eternal. He knew moments of immense joy, and he would not want to spoil your bright high. It was, in his words, such happiness that they wished it could last forever. But he honestly notes something else as well: afterward they sighed and returned to the noise of ordinary speech. A high can't last forever, and that doesn't make it any less real. For Augustine such moments were a sign of what the soul longs for. You don't have to cling to euphoria with all your might; you can remember it — so as to return to it later.
euphoria.practice: Go to a window, as Augustine did at Ostia, and look out for a minute, memorizing one detail of this high — a light, a sound, a sensation in your body. Let it be kept.

crash.text: In Book VII of the Confessions Augustine tells how for a moment he seemed to rise toward clarity and beauty — and was soon thrown back by his own weight, which he called habit. He knew from experience the painful contrast of the drop after a high. He describes this fall without despair, as the natural course of things: a soul that has lived through a high remembers it but can't live at that altitude straight away. Importantly, the memory of the high remains: Augustine writes that he carried away with him a loving memory of what he had seen. The drop doesn't cancel what was. It only shows that between the peaks lie valleys — and you can live in them too, remembering the heights.
crash.practice: Recall one thing from the high that has stayed with you — Augustine carried away "a loving memory" of what he had seen. Say aloud: "That was real" — and notice where in your body it echoes.

panic.text: In a garden in Milan Augustine was so seized by turmoil that he tore his hair and struck his forehead, unable to find a place for himself — until he went off under a fig tree and let his tears flow. He didn't describe panic in today's sense, but he knew a wave that sweeps over you and takes the body out of your control. Such a wave is genuinely frightening. And the storm subsided. It is an honest testimony: even the strongest turmoil has a peak and a subsiding. Such a wave usually rises, peaks and subsides within a few minutes. Right now you don't need to understand or decide anything — only help your body get through it.
panic.practice: Sit down or lean against something solid, like Augustine under the fig tree, press your feet into the floor and breathe out longer than you breathe in. Name aloud three objects you can see, and let tears come if they come.

dread.text: "The present of things future" — this is what Augustine called expectation: the future, he wrote in Book XI of the Confessions, does not yet exist; it lives only in our soul, now. A vague dread of what lies ahead is a heavy feeling, and there's no need to be ashamed of it; but this thought about time offers an unexpected support. So what feels like an inescapable disaster ahead is an image that lives in you at this moment. This doesn't make the feeling any less real, but it changes its scale: it is not a verdict but a state of the soul, which can change. Augustine wrote that the soul can not only scatter itself among fears about what does not yet exist, but also gather itself — return to what is here now.
dread.practice: Tell yourself: "Right now I am here, and this moment exists" — Augustine would call this gathering the soul. Name three things that are in front of you right now.

fomo.text: Augustine confesses that even a lizard catching flies or a dog chasing a hare across a field could pull him away. The sense that life is happening somewhere else is very understandable in a world of endless possibilities. Augustine described something related and called it "curiosity" (curiositas) — a thirst to see and know everything indiscriminately, not for any use but for the sake of the impression itself. For Augustine the trouble is not interest in the world but dispersal: a soul that reaches for everything spreads itself across many things and loses itself. His answer is recollection: not trying to be everywhere, but being wholly where you are. What you've missed stops burning when the present is filled with your attention.
fomo.practice: Choose one thing you're doing right now and give it all your attention for five minutes — Augustine would call this recollection. Notice what has changed.

sleepless.text: "That rest may restore tired limbs, relieve weary minds and loosen anxious sorrows" — so runs the evening hymn of Ambrose of Milan, Augustine's mentor. When the night drags on and thoughts won't let go, it is hard, and Augustine knew such nights. After his mother's death he couldn't find peace; even the baths he had hoped would help did not. Then he did fall asleep — and on waking felt that the pain had eased a little. Lying alone in bed, he remembered that very hymn of Ambrose. These lines calmed him. The night is not an enemy but a time when the soul can gradually let go of the day. Even if sleep doesn't come, you can simply lie in the quiet: rest for the body is rest too.
sleepless.practice: If you can't sleep, slowly repeat to yourself one gentle line from a poem or song you love — as Augustine repeated Ambrose's hymn. Let it sound in the rhythm of your breathing.

betrayal.text: "Even in one's own home there is no complete safety," Augustine wrote in The City of God: hidden treachery can come to light where it was least expected. Betrayal wounds especially deeply because it comes from someone you trusted. And the closer the person, he writes, the more bitter it is. He considered this one of the hardest sides of earthly life. Betrayal, for Augustine, shows not that loving and trusting were foolish, but that love inevitably makes us vulnerable. Your pain testifies that you trusted in earnest. This is not your mistake: trust is one of the finest human capacities, even when it has been abused.
betrayal.practice: Write: "I trusted because…" — and keep going. See what real things your trust was based on: for Augustine, it speaks of your capacity to love.

jealousy.text: "I was lashed with the red-hot rods of jealousy, suspicions, fears, anger and quarrels," Augustine recalls in Book III of the Confessions, remembering a youthful love in noisy Carthage. The fear of losing someone you love, burning from within, he described with astonishing honesty — and without contempt for his younger self. For Augustine jealousy is love that fears losing what it loves. In Book IV he adds an important observation: we suffer most when we cling to another mortal human being as though they were our only support and could never disappear. Jealousy is not a vice but a sign of how much this person means to you and how much you lean on them.
jealousy.practice: Ask yourself aloud: what am I afraid of losing — the person themselves, or what they mean to me? Augustine would note that the answer often shows where we cling to someone as our only support.

resentment.text: "No enemy can harm us more than our own hatred of him," Augustine writes in the Confessions. Resentment is a pain that won't go away, and it is often justified. Augustine understood its power. In the Rule for his community he speaks of anger that, if not let go, grows into hatred and turns a speck into a beam. Resentment that is carried inside and relived again and again grows in exactly this way. That's why he advises ending quarrels as quickly as possible. This doesn't mean you must forgive immediately or that the hurt means nothing. It means that resentment is your burden, and you have the right to set it down one day, when you are ready.
resentment.practice: Imagine your resentment as a stone in your hand. What is it like — heavy, sharp, cold? Ask yourself: what do I need in order to set it down one day? Augustine would not rush the answer.

heartbreak.text: Augustine writes in the Confessions that his heart, which had clung to her, was torn, wounded and bleeding. He went through one of the deepest human pains himself. In Book VI of the Confessions he tells how he had to part from the woman he had lived with for many years and with whom he had a son: she was sent away because an advantageous marriage was being arranged for him. The wound, he writes, took a long time to heal. Even the man who would later become a great philosopher couldn't get through that separation "rationally" — and didn't pretend he could. But Augustine also has a quiet observation: time does not pass idly — it flows through the soul and gradually changes it. Your pain is a testament to the depth of your love.
heartbreak.practice: Put your hand on your heart and say: "It hurts here because I loved." Stay with that for a minute, without hurrying — like Augustine, who didn't pretend he could stop loving "rationally."

impostor.text: "A seller of words" — this is what Augustine later called his Milan self, a brilliant teacher of rhetoric who taught people to speak persuasively without caring much about truth. The feeling that you're an impostor about to be exposed is agonizing, especially when you've achieved a lot — and he knew something like it. He felt uneasy about how much of his success was appearance. But there was truth in that unease too: he sensed a gap between what he showed and what he wanted to live by. Feeling like an impostor, for Augustine, doesn't prove you are unworthy of your place. Sometimes it is a voice looking for authenticity: not "who will expose me?" but "what do I want to do in earnest?"
impostor.practice: Write down one thing in your work that you do not for show but because you believe it matters. Augustine would call this the difference between a seller of words and someone seeking the truth.

self_hatred.text: Evil, for Augustine, is not an independent entity but only a lack of good — like a hole in a fabric that doesn't cancel the fabric itself. If your inner critic sounds convincing right now and you hate yourself, it is very heavy — but Augustine would not agree with that voice. In Book VII of the Confessions he arrives at a thought that turned his life around: everything that exists — precisely because it exists — is good. This means that you yourself, as a living person, are at your root good. What you hate in yourself is wounds and lacks, not your essence. The Confessions were written by a man who saw his mistakes clearly and still told his story with hope. The voice of self-hatred does not tell the truth about you.
self_hatred.practice: Name aloud one thing in yourself that doesn't need to be earned: your breath, your curiosity, your capacity to feel. For Augustine, that is the fabric, not the hole.

helplessness.text: "The mind commands the body and is obeyed at once; the mind commands itself and meets resistance," Augustine marveled in Book VIII of the Confessions. When it seems nothing can be changed, it is one of the hardest feelings, and he knew it precisely. He wanted to change, but the will could not compel itself. This was not laziness but an honest discovery: not everything can be overcome by a single effort of will. The way out, for Augustine, came through what he called grace — through help from outside, which reached him partly through other people and their stories. Even without faith you can take away this thought: helplessness is not a verdict. What doesn't work alone sometimes becomes possible with someone beside you.
helplessness.practice: Think of who could share even a small part of what now feels overwhelming, and tell them in one sentence — today or when you're ready. Other people helped Augustine.

procrastination.text: "Grant me chastity and continence — but not yet," the young Augustine prayed, and many years later he told of it honestly in the Confessions. He described putting things off perhaps better than anyone — and without malice toward himself. In Book VIII of the Confessions he recalls how for years he put off the decisive step, telling himself: "Soon, right now, just wait a little." And that "little" dragged on without end. He compared himself to someone who wants to wake up but keeps sinking back into a sweet doze. Augustine laughs at himself, but without malice: he sees that procrastination is a divided will that wants and doesn't want at the same time. For Augustine, the way out is not to scold yourself but to understand: which part of you doesn't want to — and what is it afraid of?
procrastination.practice: Ask the part of you that procrastinates — as Augustine questioned his divided will: "What are you afraid of?" Answer aloud in one sentence, in its voice.

quote.text: Grant me chastity and continence, but not yet.
quote.author: Aurelius Augustine

uprooted.text: From little Thagaste in North Africa Augustine moved to Carthage, then to Rome, then to Milan — and almost everywhere he was an outsider. He knew well the sense of being cut off from your roots. In The City of God he gave this experience a deep interpretation: human beings, he writes, are pilgrims in this world (in Latin peregrini). For Augustine this is not a curse but an honest description of the human condition: no place on earth becomes a final home, and he himself hoped for a home of another kind. But the thought can comfort outside faith too: feeling uprooted is not your personal failure but the shared lot of people. And home can be sought not only in a place, but in those you love.
uprooted.practice: Name aloud one person, one habit and one object that stay with you wherever you move. For Augustine the pilgrim, that was home on the road.

overload.text: "I have been scattered across times whose order I do not know, and my thoughts are torn by a motley tumult," Augustine writes in Book XI of the Confessions. When there's too much of everything and you're being pulled apart, it isn't a personal weakness: he knew this state from within. Time for Augustine is a "distension of the soul": we hold within us at once the memory of the past, attention to the present and the expectation of the future. When there's too much of all this, the soul is stretched to its limit. His answer is neither a sprint nor an escape, but recollection: reaching toward one thing rather than spreading yourself over many. Overload is a signal: the soul is asking not for a new effort but for a return to what matters most.
overload.practice: Close your eyes for a minute and gather yourself, as Augustine gathered his scattered soul: out of all your tasks, choose the one that truly matters today, and name it. Let the rest wait five minutes.

unreality.text: "If I am mistaken, I exist" — Augustine formulated this thought twelve centuries before Descartes. When the world or you yourself seem not quite real, it is frightening, and it's important to speak of it gently. The skeptics of his time claimed that nothing can be known for certain. Augustine answered them with a simple thought: someone who doesn't exist can't even be mistaken. And even while doubting, I know that I live, that I remember, that I want to understand. This is not an argument but a support: in the very experience of "it feels like nothing is real" there is someone who is experiencing it. Your existence is the most reliable thing you have, even when everything around seems shaky and far away.
unreality.practice: Tell yourself, as Augustine might: "I am here, I feel, I breathe." Touch something with a distinct texture — wood, fabric — and name three sensations.

quote.text: If I am deceived, I am.
quote.author: Aurelius Augustine
quote.source: The City of God, Book XI, ch. 26

awe.text: "People travel to marvel at the heights of mountains, the waves of the sea, the expanse of the ocean, the courses of the stars — and pass themselves by," Augustine wondered. Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare and precious experience, and Augustine knew it firsthand. Augustine recalls how once, gazing into the depths, he trembled with love and dread at the same time. For Augustine awe is not only admiration for the world but also an invitation to look within: in human memory and the soul he found an abyss no smaller than the sky. Your awe at the world can also become amazement that you are able to feel this way at all. Let it last.
awe.practice: Stay for a minute with what stirred your awe, and then, like Augustine, turn inward and ask yourself: what in me is able to respond like this?

relief.text: "Why is joy greater when danger came before it?" Augustine asks in Book VIII of the Confessions: sailors who have survived a storm and a sick person beginning to recover rejoice more than if there had been no trouble at all. The relief of a weight leaving is worth noticing and savoring. He also recalls the Gospel image: there is more rejoicing over the lost sheep that is found than over those that were never lost. Relief, for Augustine, is joy in which the memory of the fear you went through still echoes. That doesn't mean the trouble was necessary. But it does mean that relief is a full feeling, not just the absence of anxiety. Let it arrive completely.
relief.practice: Take a slow exhale and notice where in your body things have become lighter — like a sailor stepping ashore after a storm. Stay with that sensation for a minute.

calm.text: "The peace of all things is the tranquillity of order" — this definition from The City of God became one of Augustine's most famous. The calm you feel is a precious state, and he thought about it a great deal. For him peace is not emptiness or inactivity but a harmony in which the soul's different strivings don't pull in different directions. All his life Augustine sought such peace, and his Confessions begin precisely with the thought of a restless heart looking for a place to rest. Your calm right now is a moment when everything inside has fallen into place. There's no need to ask whether it will last. You can simply be in it.
calm.practice: Sit for a minute, noticing that right now everything is in its place: breath, body, thoughts — this is Augustine's "tranquillity of order." Nothing needs to change.

inspiration.text: "Take up and read! Take up and read!" a child's voice chanted beyond the garden wall in Milan, and Augustine opened a book lying nearby at the first page he came to. The lines seemed addressed directly to him, and that moment changed his life. Your inspiration, too, is a moment when something opens up and you want to act. For Augustine this was a sign from above. But he also has a more general thought: in the dialogue On the Teacher he argues that understanding cannot be taught by words from outside alone — a person recognizes truth from within, as if through an "inner teacher." Inspiration, then, is the moment when something inside you recognizes the truth. It's worth listening to it and writing it down while it's fresh.
inspiration.practice: Do Augustine's "take up and read": open any book nearby at a random page and read the first sentence your eyes land on. What does it say about your inspiration?

schadenfreude.text: "What was it that delighted me so?" Augustine asks himself again and again, recalling how as a teenager he stole pears with his friends and laughed at the fooled owners. Joy at someone else's failure is an awkward feeling, hard to admit even to yourself, and he confessed to something similar. The pleasure, he writes, wasn't in the pears themselves: what tickled his heart was laughing at how they had fooled the owners, who could never have imagined they were capable of it. Augustine doesn't pretend it was innocent, but he doesn't call himself a monster either. Schadenfreude, for Augustine, often feeds not on cruelty but on a thirst to feel your own strength or to belong with "your people." Having such a feeling is human. What matters is to notice which need it is really serving.
schadenfreude.practice: Ask yourself, as Augustine asked about the pears: what did this person's failure give me — a sense of justice, relief, superiority? Write down one word.

contempt.text: The "lust for domination," libido dominandi, by Augustine's observation takes a person captive: whoever wants to stand above others ends up ruled by that very lust. Contempt is a cold feeling, and sometimes it seems entirely justified; Augustine understood its roots well. Contempt is a close relative of this drive: a way of feeling superior. But Augustine also has another principle, set down in one of his letters: love people and hate their vices. You can reject an action without despising the whole person. This is not a demand to soften at once. It's an invitation to look closer: what in this person stings you — and what is your contempt protecting?
contempt.practice: Separate them in your mind, as Augustine advised: here is the action I don't accept — and here is the person, who is more than that action. Say aloud which of your values the first one touches.

disgust.text: For almost ten years Augustine was close to the Manichaeans, who regarded matter and the body as evil and the world as a battlefield of light and darkness. Disgust, that strong recoil from people, situations or even yourself, became for them a whole picture of the world. Later Augustine decisively rejected this idea: everything that exists, in his view, is at root good, and evil is only a distortion or lack of good. Disgust should not become a verdict on a whole person or a whole world. It may honestly point to something distorted and wrong — but behind it there remains what cannot be reduced to the disgusting. This matters especially if the disgust is turned on yourself.
disgust.practice: If the disgust is directed at yourself, name aloud one thing in you that remains valuable, whatever is causing the feeling — for Augustine, everything that exists is at root good.

revenge.text: Reflecting on violence, Augustine named what is truly bad in it: not so much the outward damage as "the cruelty of revenge, an unappeased and implacable spirit." When you've been hurt, wanting the one who hurt you to feel the same is understandable, and he didn't deny the strength of that feeling. For him revenge wounds first of all the one who nurses it. And in Book I of the Confessions he writes that no enemy is more dangerous than our own hatred of him. Wanting revenge is human; it says nothing about who you are. What matters is to notice what it is protecting: your pain, your dignity, your need for justice. These needs are real — and you can acknowledge them and look for a way to meet them without harming anyone.
revenge.practice: Write down what you'd like the person who hurt you to understand or feel. Then ask yourself Augustine's question: what do I myself need for this pain to ease and my spirit to be at peace?

anger_at_loved.text: Augustine's mother Monica learned not to argue with her hot-tempered husband at the height of his anger but to wait until he cooled down — and then calmly explain her side. Anger at the people close to you is one of the most uncomfortable feelings, especially when you feel ashamed of it afterward. Augustine would explain it through his central idea: all feelings are forms of love. We get angriest where we love most, because there is more expectation there and more vulnerability. Monica's example is not a call to put up with everything. It's an observation that anger and love can live side by side, and that the time for an important conversation is better chosen once the storm has passed. Anger at someone close doesn't cancel your love — it is often born of it.
anger_at_loved.practice: Say to yourself: "I'm angry with him (her) because what matters to me is…" — and finish it. And like Monica, save the important conversation for when the storm has passed.

ambivalence.text: "Man himself is a great deep," Augustine exclaims in Book IV of the Confessions. Loving someone close and not being able to stand them at once is a tangled state, and he knew such a split from the inside. In Book VIII of the Confessions he writes that there were two wills in him, the old and the new, and their struggle tore his soul apart. At the same time he argues with those who believed that two different souls, a good one and an evil one, live in a person: no, says Augustine, it is one soul that doesn't want with its whole heart. Your contradictions are not a sign that something is wrong with you or with your love. They are a sign of depth. Love and irritation can live in one heart, and one doesn't cancel the other.
ambivalence.practice: Divide a page into two columns: "what I love in him (her)" and "what I can't stand." Fill in both — not to reach a decision, but to see both truths of one soul.

guilty_relief.text: "Love your neighbor as yourself" — Augustine noted that this commandment already presupposes a right love of self. Relief you feel ashamed of is one of the most hidden feelings, rarely spoken of aloud. It comes after a breakup, a departure, even after the death of someone close who had long been ill — and it seems like a betrayal. Augustine would say: don't rush to judge yourself. For him all feelings are forms of love, and love has many layers. Relief can be love for the other, whose suffering has ended, and love for yourself, which has finally been given a respite. Relief and love don't contradict each other. They can live in one heart at the same time.
guilty_relief.practice: Tell yourself: "I feel relief — and I loved." Don't choose one: for Augustine, both loves can live in one heart.

indifference.text: As a schoolboy Augustine wept over the death of Dido in the Aeneid — and remained indifferent to his own life, which, as he later believed, was going the wrong way. When something "should" move you and inside it is quiet, it is frightening — but he knew this paradox too, and did not consider himself callous because of it. Feelings, for Augustine, don't disappear; they are directed: love is always moving somewhere, but not always where it's "supposed" to. Indifference doesn't mean you're a cold person. Perhaps your capacity to respond is tired right now, occupied with something else, or protecting you from pain that is too strong. It is a state, not a verdict.
indifference.practice: Ask yourself: where in the past few days did I feel anything at all, however small — like Augustine's tears over Dido? Note it without judging: love is always moving somewhere.

escape.text: "Where could my heart flee from my heart? Where could I go to get away from myself?" asked Augustine, who more than once dropped everything and left. The wish to leave a job, a city, a role you're sick of made sense to him, and there is nothing shameful in it. After his friend's death he moved from his native Thagaste to Carthage, because everything there reminded him of the loss. Later he secretly sailed from Carthage to Rome, tired of rowdy and insolent students. This is not a verdict on change — Augustine's moves really did change his life. It's an observation: some things we take with us. It's worth asking: what exactly do I want to get away from — and which of it will come along with me?
escape.practice: Write two lists: "what I want to leave behind" and "what I want to find." The second, Augustine would say, often tells more about the heart than the first.

forbidden_attraction.text: "I was not yet in love, but I loved to love," Augustine writes of his youth in Carthage: he was drawn to the very possibility of love. An attraction to someone unavailable or "wrong" can be confusing and unsettling. Augustine wrote a lot about desire, and his central idea is unexpected: every desire, at bottom, reaches toward some good. The disorder, for Augustine, is not in the desire itself but in its order — in how it relates to our other loves and commitments. A forbidden attraction, for Augustine, often points to what we are missing: liveliness, recognition, freedom, being seen. There's no need to judge yourself or to rush to conclusions. You can ask: what is my heart really reaching for?
forbidden_attraction.practice: Ask yourself: what does this person or this situation stand for, for me? Say one word aloud — not a name. For Augustine, that is the good the heart is reaching for.

social_anxiety.text: "Do not go outside; return into yourself — truth dwells in the inner man," Augustine wrote in Of True Religion. Shyness and fear of being judged are hard: another person's gaze feels like a verdict. Augustine admitted that he, too, depended on others' opinions. In Book X of the Confessions he examines himself closely: he is pleased when praised and stung when criticized, and he finds it hard to tell how strongly this holds him — since praise and blame are always close at hand. He doesn't pretend to be invulnerable. Others' judgment is just one view of you, and far from the most complete. You know more about yourself than can be seen from outside.
social_anxiety.practice: Before a get-together, "return into yourself" for a minute, as Augustine advised: close your eyes and say, "Their view is their view. I know more about myself." Notice what changes in your body.

uncertainty.text: "Tomorrow I'll find it; any moment now it will become clear," the thirty-year-old Augustine kept telling himself, still not understanding how to live — he tells of it in Book VI of the Confessions. Not knowing what will happen wears you out, and he knew it from experience. He wavered for years — and yet in the end he found his path. He also has a thought that can help. The future, for Augustine, does not yet exist — it exists only as expectation in our soul. So uncertainty is not an abyss ahead but the way your soul is now turned toward the unknown. Not everything has to be known in advance. For today, what can be seen today is often enough.
uncertainty.practice: Say aloud one thing you know for certain right now, and one thing you can do today. For Augustine, the future does not yet exist — but these already do.

waiting.text: Monica waited many years for change in the life of her son Augustine — and all that time she went on living, not merely waiting. Waiting — for results, an answer, news — stretches time out agonizingly, and Augustine explored exactly this sensation. In Book XI of the Confessions he writes that time is a "distension of the soul": we remember the past, see the present and expect the future all at once. Expectation, in his view, is the way the future already exists in us now. Hence his famous formula of the three kinds of present. This thought changes how we see things: waiting is not empty time that has dropped out of life, but also a way of living in the present. While you wait, there is memory and attention in you, not only expectation.
waiting.practice: While you wait, notice one thing from "the present of things present," as Augustine called it — what you see or hear right now. Stay with it for a minute.

quote.text: The present of things past, memory; the present of things present, sight; the present of things future, expectation.
quote.author: Aurelius Augustine

regret.text: "Late have I loved you, beauty so ancient and so new, late have I loved you!" Augustine exclaims in Book X of the Confessions, regretting the years spent far from what mattered most. Regret over something done or left undone is heavy, especially when it seems too late. But what sounds in it is not only bitterness but also joy: late — and yet. For Augustine the past exists only in memory, in the present. It can't be changed, but it can be reread and understood anew. The Confessions are themselves such a rereading: Augustine tells of his mistakes to see how his life grew out of them. Regret is not the end of the story but the beginning of a new way of seeing it.
regret.practice: Write down one regret, and under it what you came to understand through this experience: the Confessions are just such a rereading of the past. Even one word is enough.

quote.text: Late have I loved you, beauty so old and so new: late have I loved you.
quote.author: Aurelius Augustine

longing.text: "Half of my soul" — so Augustine, following Horace, called his dead friend, and admitted that living without him was almost unbearable. When you miss one particular person, there is a great deal of love in that pain. He wasn't embarrassed by this longing. But Augustine also has another, remarkable thought. In his sermons on the First Letter of John he writes that desire enlarges the soul: as a wineskin is stretched so that it can hold more, so longing, by deferring its fulfillment, makes the heart more spacious. Your longing is not only pain but also something that makes you deeper. It shows how much this person means to you — and that this bond is alive in you.
longing.practice: Write this person a letter you don't need to send — the way Augustine wrote of his friend in the Confessions. Tell them what you remember and what you would like to say.

world_pain.text: In 410 Rome, which had seemed eternal, was sacked — and Augustine sat down to write The City of God for people who were shaken and bewildered. Pain for the world — grim news, wars, injustice — can be almost unbearable, and he wrote in the midst of such pain. Augustine didn't deny suffering and acknowledged that disasters fall on people indiscriminately. He offered a view of history as an intertwining of two "cities" created by two kinds of love: love of self extending to contempt of God, and love of God. For him the second city lives unnoticed within every age. Even outside faith you can take away this thought: alongside the history of destruction there always runs a quiet history of care. Your pain is a sign that you haven't turned away from the world.
world_pain.practice: Find in today one small example of care or kindness — someone else's or your own — and linger on it with your eyes or your memory. For Augustine, that is the quiet "second city."

rejection.text: "Let anyone think what they like about Augustine, so long as my conscience does not accuse me before God," he once wrote, answering attacks. When you're not accepted, refused, pushed away, it wounds deeply. Augustine knew well how much in a person depends on others' approval: in the Confessions he honestly admits how praise and blame affected him. For him the main measure was not how others see you but what is really in you. This doesn't mean rejection doesn't hurt. But it does mean it doesn't determine your worth. Rejection is something someone decided, not who you are.
rejection.practice: Finish this sentence aloud: "I wasn't accepted into…, but that doesn't cancel the fact that I…" — honestly and kindly, the way one speaks of oneself before one's own conscience.

abandonment.text: "Miserable is every soul bound in friendship to mortal things: it is torn apart when it loses them," Augustine wrote after the death of his young friend. The fear of being abandoned is one of the most ancient human fears, and he knew it from both sides. He himself once secretly sailed away from his mother, leaving her weeping on the shore — and later described her grief with pain. And he knew how hard it is to lose: a friend, his mother, the woman he loved. For Augustine the fear of loss is the other side of love: we fear being deprived of what we love. But this is not a call to love less. It is an invitation to find supports that don't depend on one person's presence: in yourself, in other bonds, in what has already been between you and that nothing can undo.
abandonment.practice: Name aloud three supports in your life that don't depend on one person — even small ones. For Augustine, what has already been between you is a support too: nothing can undo it.

unrequited.text: "Give me someone who loves, and they will understand what I am saying," wrote Augustine. Unrequited love is a pain full of longing and hope at once, and he understood how strongly one can want love. In Book III of the Confessions he writes of his youth: "I was not yet in love, but I loved to love" — he was drawn to the very possibility of love. He isn't ashamed of this thirst; he describes it honestly — and so makes it understandable to others. For Augustine love is the weight of the soul, the force that moves a person. Love, for Augustine, is never in vain, even when it finds no answer: it already changes the one who loves. Your unrequited love shows how great your capacity to love is. That capacity is neither a mistake nor a weakness. It will stay with you.
unrequited.practice: Silently name three qualities you love in this person, and ask: which of them lives in me too? For Augustine, love already changes the one who loves.

humiliation.text: After the sack of Rome, in Book I of The City of God, Augustine addressed people who had suffered violence and insisted: the disgrace belongs to the one who humiliates, not to the one humiliated. Humiliation is one of the most painful feelings: it strikes at your very dignity, and afterward you want to disappear. What is done to a person against their will does not stain their soul. For Augustine purity and dignity are a matter of the will and the soul, not of what was done to a person from outside. This thought is worth repeating slowly. Humiliation does not define who you are. Your dignity has remained with you, even if it's hard to feel right now.
humiliation.practice: Repeat slowly, as Augustine would advise: "What was done to me says something about them, not about me." Say it three times, a little more slowly each time.

body_shame.text: Augustine noticed that the human body has features that seem to exist not for use but only for beauty. Dissatisfaction with your body is a heavy feeling that many people carry for years. As a young man Augustine was close to the Manichaeans — a teaching that considered the body and matter evil. Later he decisively abandoned this view. In Book XXII of The City of God he writes admiringly of the human body, of its proportion and harmony. For Augustine the body is neither a prison nor an enemy but a good creation; everything that exists is, for him, at root good. Your body is not a project to be fixed but something that already has value.
body_shame.practice: Name one thing your body did for you today: carried you, kept you warm, let you taste something. Note it with gratitude — Augustine saw the body as a good creation.

illness.text: Once a toothache robbed Augustine of his voice, and the brilliant orator wrote on a wax tablet a request to his friends to pray for him. When the body lets you down, it is hard both physically and emotionally, and he knew it firsthand and didn't pretend illness was a trifle. In Book IX of the Confessions he tells how he developed chest pains and his voice grew so weak that teaching became almost impossible. It's a touching scene: a brilliant orator deprived of his voice still found a way to ask for help. Illness is neither a defeat nor a reason for shame. It is a time when you can let others take care of you.
illness.practice: Think about what small help you could ask for today, and ask — even with a couple of words in a message, as Augustine asked with his wax tablet.

pride.text: Augustine, a brilliant orator, wrote of his talents calmly and gratefully: mind, abilities, teachers — he called all of these gifts. Pride in what you've done is a healthy and well-earned feeling. To be honest, Augustine was wary of pride. "Pride" in the sense of superbia he considered the root of many troubles — when a person puts themselves at the center of everything and forgets where their strength comes from. But superbia is not the same as joy in something done well. He didn't pretend his gifts weren't there. Healthy pride, for Augustine, is joy in what you've done that sees it as part of something larger: you were supported, you learned, you worked. Such pride doesn't separate you from others but connects you with them. And you can enjoy it with a quiet mind.
pride.practice: Write down what you're proud of, and next to it who or what helped you do it. Take joy in both: for Augustine, such pride connects rather than separates.

melancholy.text: "Why is weeping sweet to those in bitterness?" Augustine asks in Book IV of the Confessions. A bright sadness that holds both sorrow and beauty occupied him seriously. In Book III of the Confessions he marvels: why do people at the theater want to feel sad watching sorrowful stories, and even love that sadness? He gives no simple answer, but he notes that there is something in sadness that touches and draws us. Melancholy is not a malfunction but a particular way of feeling the world: it holds a sensitivity to what passes and a love for what has been. You don't have to drive it away. Let it stay for a while.
melancholy.practice: Put on music that matches your mood and simply listen, changing nothing — Augustine wept listening to hymns in Milan and called those tears good.
